name: Ben Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the first year of a primary teaching degree in a university town about two hours from where I grew up. Weeks are lectures on child development and maths teaching, one school visit on Tuesdays where I help in a Year 3 class, and a football session on Wednesday evenings. My parents cover rent and fees, so I only work a few hours at a climbing gym front desk. The school visit is the best bit. The essay deadlines are the worst.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a relief that the hype was hype, but that it doesn't help schools. Teachers are already stretched, and a few time-saving tools aren't going to change that. I'd tell my course mates to keep an eye on what the tools actually do before anyone gets excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel okay. Teaching is people, and a class of thirty seven-year-olds isn't going to be run by a chatbot. I use AI now and then to draft lesson ideas and it's useful but it's wrong about a third of the time. I'd call that a decent helper, not a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the degree and the Tuesday visits, and keep using AI for first drafts of plans. I'd probably ask my school mentor how she uses it, to see what's realistic. I'd also put my climbing gym wages into a savings account for a trip next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, honestly. There's a low hum of worry about pay in teaching, but that's always been there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the low hum about, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teacher pay and workload. My aunt left primary teaching after six years. She said it was the paperwork. If AI really cut the paperwork, I'd be happy, because my aunt left teaching over marking and reports, not over the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So would you want more AI in schools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the paperwork, yes. For anything that touches the children's learning, I'd want teachers to decide, not a company.

Check what the tools **actually do** before anyone gets excited.
think: A class of thirty **seven-year-olds** won't be run by a chatbot.
AI is a **helper**, wrong about a third of the time.
do: Keep the **Tuesday school visits** and use AI for first drafts.
Ask my **mentor** how she uses it.
Save climbing-gym wages for a **summer trip**.
feel: Pretty **calm**, with a low hum about teacher pay.
S0.quote: If AI really cut the paperwork, I'd be happy, because my aunt left teaching over marking and reports, not over the children.
fieldNote: He uses AI **sensibly** and tests it against experience.
His aunt's story shapes his view of **teacher burnout**.
He draws a line between paperwork and children's learning.

steps.text: Keep the Tuesday school visit and the Year 3 class
Ask my school mentor how she uses AI for plans
Move climbing gym wages into a summer trip fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the sensible response is training for teachers, paid for by the government, and a say in what gets bought. I'd tell my course mates that schools need rules about AI before it spreads, not after. I'd also argue for smaller classes so teachers can spend time with children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think teaching is safer than most degrees, but not unaffected. Lesson planning, marking and parent emails are thinking tasks, and those are the first to go. That could mean fewer teaching assistants, who are often on low pay, and bigger classes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with the degree but pick up more experience with AI planning tools, so I'm the newer teacher who can use them well. I'd join the student teachers' union branch. I'd also volunteer at a homework club to see what children actually need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My own job looks safe, but the people around it feel less so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The teaching assistants. Mrs Okafor, the teaching assistant on my school visit, has been in the class eleven years. A head teacher could still cut that job to save money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably ask her what she'd want me to say to our course. She'd know better than I would.

say: Teachers need **paid training** from the government and a say in what gets bought.
Schools need **rules** about AI before it spreads, not after.
think: Lesson planning, marking and parent emails are **thinking tasks**, so they go first.
**Teaching assistants** could be cut and classes could grow.
do: Build **AI planning** skills so I'm a useful new teacher.
feel: **Uneasy**, as my job looks safe but those around it don't.
S1.quote: Mrs Okafor, the teaching assistant on my school visit, has been in the class eleven years. A head teacher could still cut that job to save money.
fieldNote: His worry is for **colleagues**, not himself.
He sees AI as a **budget lever** for head teachers.
He wants teaching assistants' views at the centre.

steps.text: Practise AI lesson-planning tools on Tuesday school visits
Join the student teachers' union branch this term
Start volunteering at the Thursday homework club

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that two years is nowhere near enough for a school system. I'd say publicly that governments should freeze big decisions on AI in schools until teachers, parents and councils have talked. I'd go to a march if one was organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm scared that the degree will be worth less than I thought. If thinking work is done for free by AI, then schools might shrink their budgets, and robots might do hands-on classroom stuff by 2031. I just don't know whether a human teacher stays at the front of a class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the course for the first year at least, because I have no better plan. I'd work more hours at the gym, build a cushion, and talk with my parents about whether to pause fees until we see where things are heading. I'd also ask my tutor which schools are hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I have people backing me, but I can't see what I'd be training for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes about your choices when there's a two-year warning rather than ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten I'd keep going and adapt. With two I'd have no real time to adapt, and I'd probably stop thinking about a long career and start thinking about money and family. My parents have a little room, and I'd want to use that carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a moment you'd actually leave the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the university said teaching placements were being cut, I'd go. I won't spend three more years on something that has no job at the end.

S2.quote: If the university said teaching placements were being cut, I'd go. I won't spend three more years on something that has no job at the end.
fieldNote: He has a clear **exit trigger**: cuts to placements.
His family cushion gives him **room to pause**.
The two-year clock turns him from adapting to **protecting money**.

steps.text: Work extra hours at the climbing gym to build a cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to push for a teacher-led plan, and I'd want my union to lead on it. I'd write to my local politician and try to start a conversation with my course group about what teaching looks like in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd graduate in 2029, teach for a few years, then face robots that might do some classroom tasks. It's strange, because I'd be just starting my career as everything changes. I'd feel a bit like I'd bought a train ticket right before the line closed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, but add a second string, like youth work or a sports coaching qualification. I'd keep using AI tools so I'm not behind. I'd put money into a stocks and shares account my gran opened for me, and leave it alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not frozen. I can see a path, just a narrow one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years compare with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a lot less frightening. Two years is panic, five is planning. I'd have a degree and a few years of experience before robots could really reach classrooms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And compared with ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten would feel like plenty of room. At five I'd be asking if my first job is permanent, and I'd want a backup like coaching in case I'm one of the first cut.

I'd write to my **local politician** and start a course-group conversation.

It's like buying a **train ticket** before the line closes.
do: Finish the degree and add a **sports coaching** qualification.
Keep using **AI tools** to stay current.
Leave money in the **shares account** my gran opened.
feel: **Uneasy** but not frozen; I can see a narrow path.
S3.quote: Two years is panic, five is planning. I'd have a degree and a few years of experience before robots could really reach classrooms.
fieldNote: He uses **planning** as the key idea for five years.

His train-ticket image shows the contradiction of his degree.

steps.text: Finish the primary teaching degree and graduate in 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's the version where everyone can calm down. A decade lets teacher training catch up and a good government could rewrite the curriculum around things children will need. I'd be loud about it in my course group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel pretty good. I'd be teaching for years before robots do hands-on work in 2039, and AI might take the paperwork off teachers like my aunt. I think that could make the job better, not worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and teach for a few years, then decide about a masters in education or school leadership. I'd keep an eye on how AI changes lesson planning and take a short course to stay ahead. I'd also try to save a deposit for a flat by 25.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. Careful, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you plan differently for a family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd feel safer having kids with ten years of runway, and I'd want a partner with a different kind of job, in case teaching changes. That's not romantic but it's honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger sibling who wanted to teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teaching with a side skill is a safer bet than teaching alone, so I'd tell a younger sibling who wanted to teach to learn something else too.

say: A decade lets **teacher training** catch up with the change.
A good government can rewrite the **curriculum** around what children need.
think: I'd teach for years before **robots** in 2039, and AI might cut paperwork.
do: Teach a few years then consider a **masters** in education.
Take a short **AI course** to stay ahead.
S4.quote: Teaching with a side skill is a safer bet than teaching alone, so I'd tell a younger sibling who wanted to teach to learn something else too.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him treat AI as a **chance** to cut paperwork.
He ties the picture to **family timing** and a partner's job.
His advice is practical, not ideological.

steps.text: Teach for three years then apply for a masters in education
Take a short course in AI lesson tools
Save a flat deposit by the age of 25

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because a school can't change in two years. What would help is a clear teacher-led plan from the government, paid training, and honest numbers about teaching jobs, so students like me can choose with open eyes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Teaching is still about children, and somebody has to be in the room when a seven-year-old doesn't understand fractions. I'd like people who run schools to talk to student teachers. We're in classrooms every week and we see what actually helps.

headlineQuote: Teaching is still about children, and somebody has to be in the room when a seven-year-old doesn't understand fractions.
portrait: Ben is a first-year **primary teaching** student who uses AI now and then for lesson ideas.
He is progressive and thinks schools need **rules and training** before tools spread.
His parents pay everything, so he worries about **teaching jobs**, not money.
He has a clear exit trigger: cuts to **school placements**.
He is calmest with ten years and most anxious with two.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because schools can't change in **two years**.
whatWouldHelp: A **teacher-led plan** and paid training from government.
